hero.headline: Fertilizer ban takes effect across Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties
hero.teaser: A ban on any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen is in place across Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties to reduce nutrient runoff during the rainy season.
hero.body:
Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties have a ban on any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen. Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, said the ban is to help reduce nutrient rich run off during the rainy season, which can cause algae blooms. Those blooms could disrupt waterways like the Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River.

"It can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife," said Skaggs. "At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health." Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, said a good alternative during the ban is using composting for your garden and landscaping. "It can be like a small trash can," said Ricketts. "That is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape."

cards.headline: Single-vehicle crash on Donald Ross Road in Jupiter kills one person Sunday morning
cards.body:
A single-vehicle crash on Donald Ross Road in Jupiter Sunday morning killed one person, according to Jupiter police officials. The crash happened just before 6 a.m. when the driver came over railroad tracks, lost control of the vehicle, and struck a tree.

Police confirmed one adult male died in the crash but are withholding the victim's name pending notification of next of kin. The preliminary information indicates the driver lost control after traveling over the railroad tracks.

Both eastbound and westbound lanes of Donald Ross Road between Military Trail and Alternate A1A were closed for several hours as crash investigators worked the scene. The roadway has since reopened to traffic.

The Jupiter Police Department is continuing to investigate the circumstances that led to the fatal crash. Investigators remained at the scene throughout the morning to gather evidence and reconstruct the sequence of events.

The pastor's identity and the specific church affiliation have not been released. Fort Pierce police are investigating the case involving the foster children who were removed from the home.

cards.headline: Indiantown brush fire grows to 125 acres, 99% contained after weekend flare-up
cards.teaser: A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated to 125 acres over the weekend before being brought under near-total control, according to Martin County F.
cards.body:
A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated over the weekend before being brought under near-total control, according to Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Forest Service. The incident began on Friday, June 5, when MCFR firefighters responded to a rapidly developing brush fire in the 2600 block of Southwest Warfield Boulevard just before 3:30 p.m. Crews quickly contained the blaze at approximately 37.8 acres, with no reported injuries and no structures threatened at the time. The Florida Forest Service assisted on scene by establishing plow lines to help stop the spread of flames. MCFR's drone team played a key role in identifying remaining hotspots and confirming full containment before crews cleared the area.

By Saturday, June 6, the situation escalated significantly when crews returned to battle a much larger 120-acre brush fire in the same general area. Officials believe the fire rekindled from the previous day's incident. Shifting winds and dense vegetation contributed to rapid fire growth, prompting a large-scale response from MCFR, FFS, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Firefighters worked to protect nearby structures as smoke spread across the area, though officials confirmed there was no broader threat to the public. Residents were advised to expect smoky conditions throughout the weekend. The fire reached approximately 125 acres in total and is 99% contained as of Sunday morning. The investigation into the fire's origin remains ongoing.

cards.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration at Palm Beach State College
cards.teaser: 35 students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth and young adults served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit.
cards.body:
35 students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth and young adults served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit. ChildNet supports foster kids and young men and women through education, adoptions and independent living resources.

Among the graduates were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, both of whom lost a parent and turned to ChildNet for support. The organization equipped them with the resources they needed to move forward. Diaz shared a message for others in similar situations: "Belief that you're going to be big one day and just put effort into it, never give up on school and never give up on dreams. If you like push past with the pain and just keep trying hard." Saintfort echoed that message, saying "Believe that you'll make it, then you're gonna make it and stuff." Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, reflected on the evening's significance: "This evening is the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet, DCF and especially the kids who have worked so hard. We are to celebrate them!" Diaz is already enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College, where she hopes to become a doctor. Saintfort plans to pursue a vocational program to become a plumber.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie 9-year-old starts junior chess club at Morningside Library
cards.teaser: Orion Jean Baptiste, a 9-year-old from Port St. Lucie, has launched a new juniors chess club that now meets every Friday at the Morningside Library with more than 36 members.
cards.body:
A new juniors chess club has launched in Port St. Lucie, inspired by 9-year-old Orion Jean Baptiste, who wanted to share his love of the game with his community. Baptiste's passion for chess began at age 5, playing alongside family members. "I just wanted kids to learn about chess," Baptiste said. "Everybody's more focused on like tech stuff. I'm hoping that more people have respect for board games."

Diana Cowan Kempton, the club's program director, believes chess can help develop the next generation of focused and strategic thinkers. "[It] will help to build leaders or members that are more focused, more patient, more strategic and thoughtful in their decision [making]," Kempton said. The Atlantis Chess Club is attracting players of all skill levels and has already enrolled more than 36 juniors at the Port St. Lucie Morningside Library, where it meets every Friday. The club will soon expand with two additional programs at the Fenn Center in Fort Pierce.

cards.headline: Pride on the Block raises funds for Transpire Help in West Palm Beach
cards.teaser: Pride on the Block filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, which provides substance use treatment, mental health care, and housing to LGBTQ+ individuals.
cards.body:
A vibrant celebration of love and identity filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as Pride on the Block brought together neighbors, allies, and activists in support of the LGBTQ+ community. The event serves as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, a non-profit organization that provides crucial services including substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals.

Donna Weinberger, founder of Transpire Help, said the event creates a space where attendees can feel celebrated and safe. She noted that a significant portion of the community lacks health insurance or funds to access traditional treatment resources. Weinberger said the fundraiser is more important than ever, as cuts to government funding have slashed the number of people the organization can help in half. For performer Liam Chambers, the event carries deep personal meaning. Chambers credits Transpire Help with helping turn his life around, saying: "I am three years sober and now I can get on the stage, I'm a drag king and I wouldn't have been able to do it without them."

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway in Vero Beach to make way for mixed-use development
cards.teaser: Crews began taking down portions of the Indian River Mall this week to make way for a revitalization project for the shopping center.
cards.body:
This week, crews began demolishing portions of the Indian River Mall in Vero Beach to make way for a revitalization project. Project manager Joseph Scarfone said the first phase involves taking down the Macy's and the former Sears location. Neighbors gathered in the parking lot to watch the demolition, with reactions ranging from relief to cautious optimism. "I'm really happy they're tearing this down," said neighbor Mary Alice Stopyra. "It's just degraded over time." Mark Manera, who has visited the mall for years, described it as "the death of a beautiful building" and "more like a graveyard," noting "a steady decline year after year after year." However, Manera expressed hope for the future. "If that brings new life, new jobs, new opportunity, that's wonderful," he said.

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a new sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center featuring around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants, and possible residential spaces. "They're not going to see a dead mall for the last 12 years that was getting cobwebs," Scarfone said. "It's a city within a city." He hopes to complete the first phase by 2027, though the team is still working on obtaining permits for the remainder of the project.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart over alleged parasites in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections after finding live worms in SpaghettiOs purchased at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee.
cards.body:
Mary Hubbard from Okeechobee County claims she and her daughter found live worms in their SpaghettiOs and developed parasitic infections and other medical complications as a result. The alleged incident occurred in June 2024 when Hubbard purchased the product at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. According to her lawsuit against Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart, she discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food.

Hubbard documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the food product, according to her attorneys. The lawsuit alleges the companies failed to properly inspect the product and seeks $50,000 in damages. Campbell Soup Co. said the claims lack merit, while Walmart stated it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance program overwhelmed with 8,000 calls per month
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program receives about 600 applications in the first couple of hours they're open each month, with nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance monthly.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding for its Emergency Rental Assistance Program, designed to help residents who can't pay rent. But each month, demand overwhelms available resources. "We're doing what we can to prioritize and serve those who are most needy but the demand it far outweighs the resources that are available," said program director Dr. James Green. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Green said the recent surge in applications stems partly from rising costs of living, including housing, gas, and food.

Applications open at the beginning of each month but fill rapidly. "There are nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month based on our data combined with 211. We currently have about 800 applications in the queue for rental assistance right now. We typically receive about 600 applications the first couple of hours they're open," Green explained. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked CLOSED due to high demand. Green urges anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability. For those unable to access the county's program, 211 is available 24/7 to connect residents with nonprofits and other assistance programs in the area.

cards.headline: Florida could ban Fourth of July fireworks due to severe drought conditions
cards.teaser: State leaders are weighing whether to ban fireworks for the Fourth of July's 250th anniversary celebration as Florida faces drought conditions more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide ban was enacted.
cards.body:
Florida's Fourth of July celebrations could look very different this year as state leaders weigh whether to ban fireworks due to severe drought conditions. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services says this year's drought is even more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was put in place. The entire state of Florida is at least abnormally dry, with areas including Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning about the possibility of a ban in May. "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about obviously, potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time," Simpson said. Simpson acknowledged the significance of this year's 250th anniversary celebration but urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, owner Bill Murphy reported increased customer activity ahead of the holiday. Murphy said the store monitors drought conditions closely but remains cautiously optimistic about rain in the forecast. The Department of Agriculture said a fireworks ban would be a last resort.

cards.headline: Florida voters divided on property tax proposal ahead of November ballot
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide this November whether to raise the homestead exemption for homeowners, a proposal that would need 60% approval to pass.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to raise the homestead exemption to roll back property taxes, a proposal drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents. The ballot measure requires 60% approval to pass. A similar proposal to raise the homestead exemption failed in 2018. How much money cities and counties would lose remains unclear, and where budget cuts would fall if the measure passes is still unknown.

Homeowners expressed divided views on the proposal. Rosabella Olivares, a shopper in West Palm Beach, expressed concern about reduced funding. "There's going to be less money ... because everything is expensive now," Olivares said. Brian Edington supports the idea because it benefits permanent Florida residents and said he is comfortable with local governments spending less, pointing to his neighborhood's trash service as an example where cuts could be made. A resident identified as Stan said he does not want funding eliminated entirely, noting that "infrastructure and all that stuff is important." Renters expressed more skepticism about the proposal. One resident interviewed along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach on Friday said savings would not reach renters. "Pretty sure they're going to raise the rent on everybody, all the renters," the renter said.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island officials warn erosion could split island in half at Peck Lake
cards.teaser: A new state report warns that nearly the entire coastline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, with the ocean potentially breaking through at Peck Lake and splitting the island in half.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely that the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breach could turn a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A similar breach occurred during a storm in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said a future breach could upend ecosystems that depend on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater. The consequences extend beyond the shoreline to conservation lands and historical sites. At risk is the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, along with wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Over 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these areas, and erosion is threatening mangrove swamps critical for habitat and coastal protection.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town fights erosion through constant beach renourishment. In April 2025, the town completed a major project dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field said oceanfront homes are not in immediate danger because of this work, but characterized the approach as temporary: "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over." The town spends approximately $3 million annually in taxpayer funds on beach renourishment. Field warned that without continued state and federal funding, "We would have cataclysmic erosion."

hero.headline: 9-year-old Port St. Lucie boy launches junior chess club at Morningside Library
hero.body:
Orion Jean Baptiste, a 9-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, has started a junior chess club to introduce other young people to a game he has loved since age 5. Baptiste learned to play chess by spending time with family members and developed a passion for the game that he now wants to share with his community. The Atlantis Chess Club meets every Friday at the Morningside Library in Port St. Lucie and welcomes players of all skill levels.

The club has already attracted more than 36 junior members in a short time. Diana Cowan Kempton, the club's program director, believes chess can help shape the next generation of young people. According to Kempton, the game helps develop leaders and community members who are more focused, patient, strategic and thoughtful when making decisions. Baptiste himself sees value in promoting board games during an era when many young people are drawn to technology and screens. "I'm hoping that more people have respect for board games," Baptiste said. "Everybody's more focused on like tech stuff."

Families in the community have embraced the club for its positive atmosphere and educational benefits. Thomas Furlong brought his two children to the club because he saw it as an ideal opportunity for his daughter to learn the game and his son to improve his skills. Furlong also appreciated the friendly competition it created between his children. His daughter Francesca Furlong, who recently joined the club, enjoys the social aspect of playing with other children. "Playing with other kids" is what she likes most about being a member, she said.

The Atlantis Chess Club's success in Port St. Lucie has led to expansion plans. The club will soon launch two additional programs at the Fenn Center in Fort Pierce, extending Baptiste's mission to more young people in the area. Through his initiative, Baptiste is demonstrating how one person's passion for a game can build community connections and inspire others to develop skills like patience, strategic thinking and focus. His simple goal of helping kids learn about chess has grown into something much larger.

cards.headline: Pride on the Block fundraiser supports Transpire Help services in West Palm Beach
cards.teaser: Pride on the Block brought together neighbors, allies, and activists at The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday to support Transpire Help, a nonprofit providing substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals.
cards.body:
Pride on the Block filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, a non-profit organization that provides substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals. The event brought together community members and allies to celebrate identity and support the organization's work. "It's such a great feeling to be around people in our community and express how you want to be represented," said Cortney Salley, an LGBTQ+ community member. Donna Weinberger, founder of Transpire Help, said the event creates a space where attendees can feel celebrated. "People can come and be filled with unity and joy and happiness and be able to be in one spot and feel safe," Weinberger said.

For performer Liam Chambers, the event held deep personal meaning. Chambers said he is three years sober and credited Transpire Help with his recovery. "I am a drag king and I wouldn't have been able to do it without them," Chambers said. Weinberger emphasized the organization's critical role, noting that many in the LGBTQ+ community lack health insurance or funds to access treatment. She said government funding cuts have slashed the number of people Transpire Help can assist in half. Jack Cesivon said the organization has helped people with no other support. Jake Jayalin Eggert described the event as creating authentic community where people feel heard and seen.

hero.headline: Beetlejuice musical closes Sunday at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
hero.teaser: The Broadway hit runs through June 7 at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall, bringing spooky humor and over-the-top visuals to Palm Beach County.
hero.body:
Beetlejuice the musical has landed at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach, running June 2 through June 7. Actor Ryan Stajmiger steps into the iconic striped suit to play the mischievous demon beloved from Tim Burton's 1988 film. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a strange and unusual teen, whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is laughing with the audience. He gets to break the fourth wall and communicate directly to the audience, sharing moments with them. Very early in the run, he experienced an unexpected moment when he was wearing two wigs and the second wig came off with the first wig, leaving him bald for an entire scene.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50 and are available at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

cards.headline: Lake Worth Beach to host 80-mile ocean paddle crossing for cystic fibrosis awareness
cards.body:
More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the open Atlantic Ocean this June to raise awareness and funds for families living with cystic fibrosis in the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis. According to event founder Travis Suit, participants will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13, arriving at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. The endurance trek benefits the Piper's Angels Foundation, which Suit established in honor of his daughter, Piper, diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10, with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On Thursday, participants take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and a community buffet dinner. Friday brings a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before launch night. All paddlers are required to wear a U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device, waterproof whistle, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, and mandatory safety meetings will be held. Paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, while crew or virtual participants have a $500 minimum. Final contributions are due July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to cheer paddlers during a daylong beach celebration marking their arrival.

hero.headline: Gov. DeSantis appoints five trustees to St. Johns River State College board
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis announced appointments and reappointments to the St. Johns River State College District Board of Trustees this month. Alexandria Hill and Kevin Payne were newly appointed to the board, while Richard Komando, Willard "Judd" Sapp Jr. and Tammy "Chereese" Stewart were reappointed. The Florida Senate must confirm these appointments before they become official.

St. Johns River State College operates three campuses across Orange Park, Palatka and St. Augustine, serving approximately 8,000 students combined. Hill brings legal expertise to the board as a partner in the Driver, McAfee, Hawthorne Dibenow law firm. She is active in the Clay County community and serves on the Clay County Development Authority. Hill earned a bachelor's degree in finance and marketing from Stetson University and a law degree from the University of Florida. Payne works as senior manager of contracting for Imagine 360 health insurance company and serves as president of the Jacksonville Association of Health Underwriters. He holds a bachelor's degree in accounting from the University of Texas and an MBA from Oklahoma City University.

Komando brings extensive legal experience to the board as a partner in the Bradley, Garrison Komando law firm on the First Coast. He previously served as circuit director and statewide general counsel for the Fourth Judicial Circuit Guardian ad Litem Office for Northeast Florida and worked as an assistant state attorney in that circuit. Komando holds a bachelor's degree in criminal justice and an MBA from Florida State University, along with a law degree from Loyola University. Sapp is a Navy veteran who previously served on the St. Johns County Day School Board of Trustees. He earned a bachelor's degree from Florida State University.

Stewart currently serves as assistant county manager for the Clay County Commission and was previously elected to that position. She is involved in multiple local organizations, including the Clay County Development Authority, Clay County Cattlemen Association, Clay County Farm Bureau and the Florida Planning and Zoning Association. Stewart earned a bachelor's degree from Texas A&M University and a master's degree in educational leadership and administration from the University of North Florida. These board members will help guide the college's operations and strategic direction across its three-county service area.

cards.headline: Rep. Kat Cammack presents flags at Florida Law Enforcement Officers Hall of Fame induction
cards.teaser: Five officers were inducted into the Florida Law Enforcement Officers Hall of Fame in Tallahassee on Saturday, with Rep. Kat Cammack presenting American flags to the honorees and families.
cards.body:
Rep. Kat Cammack presented American flags to inductees and families during the Florida Law Enforcement Officers Hall of Fame ceremony Saturday in Tallahassee. The North Florida Representative for CD 3 was joined by Florida Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Mark Glass for the induction of Larry Corgin, Michael "Mick" McHale, the late O.L. Raulerson, the late Harrel Reid and Daniel Slaughter. Cammack noted that law enforcement is a calling and a commitment to run toward danger when others run away, including a willingness to miss birthdays, holidays, anniversaries and family dinners.

The inductees had distinguished service in Florida law enforcement. Corgin is the retired assistant chief in the South Miami Police Department who served for nearly 40 years and volunteered in New York City to support police in the days immediately following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. McHale is a retired sergeant with the Sarasota Police Department who serves as president of the National Association of Police organizations. Raulerson was the only person elected sheriff in two different Florida counties, serving in Highlands and Okeechobee counties over four decades. Reid served as sheriff of Hamilton County for nine consecutive terms over 36 years, the longest serving sheriff in state history. Slaughter is the retired chief of the Clearwater Police Department with a 30-year career who helped develop the Real-Time Operations Center, noted as a model for mental health response in law enforcement.

cards.headline: Jay Collins presses Byron Donalds for gubernatorial debate as primary approaches
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial candidate Jay Collins is calling on front-runner Byron Donalds to debate, appearing on Fox News to criticize what he called the Naples Congressman's unwillingness to engage challengers.
cards.body:
Jay Collins acknowledged the long odds he faces in the Republican gubernatorial primary and is calling for a debate with front-runner Byron Donalds to close the gap. During an appearance on Fox News Sunday Morning Futures, the retired Green Beret and former state Senator compared Donalds to a former president in his unwillingness to debate challengers. Collins argued that Donalds told the entire state he will not debate because the Republican Party of Florida set criteria that no one has seen, and that he wants Republicans to coalesce behind him. "Last I checked, we don't coronate people in America. There was a whole 1776 thing about that," Collins said, adding that candidates must fight for the nomination rather than expect it.

The financial and polling disparities between the candidates underscore Collins' challenge. Donalds has raised roughly $81 million during his campaign, while Collins raised approximately $1.75 million through the end of March. Former House Speaker Paul Renner, another establishment candidate, raised more than $6 million through that same period. Fundraising reports covering activity through May are due June 10. Polls show Donalds leading by significant margins in every survey. The Democratic field consolidated after Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings withdrew for health reasons, leaving former Congressman David Jolly as the presumptive nominee.

cards.headline: Trump defends Iran military action, dismisses campaign promise of no new wars
cards.teaser: President Donald Trump said he did not guarantee there would be no wars if he returned to office, defending ongoing military actions against Iran in an NBC interview.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump dismissed claims that his military action against Iran contradicts his 2024 campaign promise of "no new wars," saying in an NBC "Meet the Press" interview that aired Sunday he "didn't guarantee" there would be no wars. Trump defended the conflict as necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, characterizing it as "doing the world a service" and noting it has lasted three months rather than being endless. When pressed by NBC's Kristen Welker on his statements about building "the strongest military in the world," Trump said as a candidate "I didn't promise anything."

Trump also defended a now-scrapped $1.776 billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund" that the Department of Justice announced Wednesday it was abandoning. The fund was part of a settlement resolving Trump's lawsuit against the IRS over leaked tax returns. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department scrapped the plan after a judge paused it and both Democrats and some Republicans raised concerns about oversight and potential payouts to January 6 Capitol riot participants. Trump told NBC he considered the fund "a great idea." Trump ended the interview abruptly when Welker pressed him for evidence supporting his repeated claims of mass fraud in California's primary vote count from Tuesday.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds defends Trump Iran actions on Newsmax, calls theocracy untrustworthy
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds defended President Trump's Iran policy Sunday, saying the President made the right call to stop the country from acquiring nuclear weapons.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds defended President Donald Trump's actions against Iran during an appearance on Newsmax's Sunday Agenda, arguing that Trump's approach does not contradict his campaign promise to avoid starting foreign wars. Donalds said the President had to address the immediate reality of Iran's nuclear ambitions. "The Iranians were enriching material. They were taking it to weapons-grade nuclear material, and they had to be stopped," Donalds said. He characterized the situation as unique among nations worldwide and noted that Trump said much of the action has occurred under a ceasefire with an effective blockade in place.

The Naples Congressman said Iran's theocratic dictatorship has repeatedly lied about its ballistic missile capabilities, claiming a 4,000-mile range that is twice what Iran previously stated and capable of reaching Europe and U.S. bases there. Donalds emphasized that Iran cannot be trusted, citing 47 years of unreliable behavior and stating the country is committed to radical Sharia law, which he said is incompatible with Western civilization. During his NBC Meet the Press appearance, Trump said he did not promise to avoid all wars, stating instead that he opposes endless conflicts. "We've been doing this for three months. Much of it has been under the form of a pretty good form of ceasefire," Trump said, adding that the threat is largely over.

Orion Jean Baptiste, a 9-year-old from Port St. Lucie, founded a new juniors chess club at the local library after developing a passion for the game at age 5 while playing with family. "I just wanted kids to learn about chess," Baptiste said. He hopes to shift focus away from technology toward board games, saying "Everybody's more focused on like tech stuff. I'm hoping that more people have respect for board games."

Diana Cowan Kempton, the club's program director, believes chess will benefit the next generation by building "leaders or members that are more focused, more patient, more strategic and thoughtful in their decision making." cards.headline: Indiantown brush fire grows to 125 acres over weekend, now 99% contained
cards.teaser: A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated over the weekend before being brought under near-total control, according to Martin County Fire Rescue an.
cards.body:
A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated over the weekend before being brought under near-total control, according to Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Forest Service. The incident started on Friday, June 5, when firefighters responded to a rapidly developing brush fire in the 2600 block of Southwest Warfield Boulevard just before 3:30 p.m. Crews quickly contained the blaze at approximately 37.8 acres, with no reported injuries and no structures threatened. The Florida Forest Service assisted by establishing plow lines to help stop the spread of flames, while Martin County Fire Rescue's drone team identified remaining hotspots and confirmed full containment before crews cleared the area. Officials noted the fire's cause was unknown, though early indications suggested it may have been a holdover fire, where a lightning strike could have smoldered underground for days before igniting visible flames.

By Saturday, June 6, the situation escalated significantly when crews returned to battle a much larger 120-acre brush fire in the same general area. Officials believe the fire rekindled from the previous day's incident. Shifting winds and dense vegetation contributed to rapid fire growth, prompting a large-scale response from Martin County Fire Rescue, the Florida Forest Service, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Firefighters worked to protect nearby structures as smoke spread across the area, though officials confirmed there was no broader threat to the public. The fire reached approximately 125 acres total and is 99% contained as of Sunday morning, with the Florida Forest Service remaining in the area to monitor conditions and ensure no further flare-ups occur. The investigation into the fire's origin remains ongoing.

cards.headline: Pride on the Block fills West Palm Beach with celebration and support for LGBTQ+ community
cards.teaser: A vibrant celebration of love and identity filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as Pride on the Block brought together neighbors, allies, and activists in support of the LGBTQ+ community.
cards.body:
Pride on the Block brought together neighbors, allies, and activists at The Peach in West Palm Beach on Saturday to celebrate the LGBTQ+ community and support Transpire Help, a non-profit organization providing substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals. The event serves as the organization's largest fundraiser. Donna Weinberger, founder of Transpire Help, said the event creates a space where attendees can feel celebrated. "People can come and be filled with unity and joy and happiness and be able to be in one spot and feel safe," Weinberger said.

For performers like Liam Chambers, the event carries deep personal meaning. Chambers credits Transpire Help with turning his life around, saying he is three years sober and now able to perform as a drag king. Weinberger noted that a significant portion of the community, especially gender diverse individuals, lack health insurance or funds to access treatment. The fundraiser has become increasingly critical as cuts to government funding have slashed the number of people Transpire Help can assist in half.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County parents and commissioner respond to teen takeover trend at Wellington mall
cards.teaser: A social media post promoting a teen takeover at the Wellington Green Mall gained nearly 100,000 views, prompting the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office to step in with an increased law enforcement presence.
cards.body:
A social media post promoting a teen takeover at Wellington Green Mall gained nearly 100,000 views, prompting the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office to increase law enforcement presence at the mall on Friday. Teen takeovers are large gatherings of teens at malls, beaches or parks that typically devolve into violence. The trend has spread across Florida, including an event in Clearwater at the end of May that resulted in widespread property damage, fights and the shooting of a 17-year-old. Shoppers including Savanna Restrepo, who was picking up her son Isaac from summer camp, noticed the heightened police presence. Restrepo said she had seen posts circulating online about the event ahead of time and found the visible police presence reassuring. Fellow parent Eric Delgado said the response was necessary.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Greg Weiss said community safety is a priority but pointed to a root cause: kids need something to do during summer break. Weiss said parents should fill teens' time with activities at community rec centers in cities and county facilities, or sports programs. He acknowledged that summer camp costs can be a barrier and noted that Palm Beach County offers scholarship opportunities for summer camps. Weiss emphasized that parental involvement is the bottom line, telling parents to know what their kids are doing and stay in contact with them.
